thesis: This episode argues that investors should emulate the long-term holding strategies of major families like the Gates, Walton, and Google founders, who maintain significant stakes in their respective companies (MSFT, AMZN, AAPL, WMT, GOOGL) without trimming. It suggests that these concentrated positions are justified by the enduring value of the businesses and the founders' confidence, while also highlighting Berkshire Hathaway's massive capital reserves and energy investments as a model for scale. The thesis is thin, focusing primarily on the 'do nothing' philosophy for top holdings and the specific examples of family-owned companies that have held their stock for decades.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests holding Apple without trimming, viewing it as a significant part of the portfolio with no immediate concerns for the next 5-10 years.
claims.quote: What do you think you would do in their seat at this point? Would you start to trim this big position? Or did you hold on thinking this might be the world's first $10 trillion dollar company? I think first $5 trillion, too.

claims.claim: The speaker advises doing nothing with Apple unless there is a permanent secular decline, noting no concerns on the horizon for the next 5-10 years.
claims.quote: The framework you use when you are a large owner of Apple, or let's say the founder of Apple, let's say Steve Jobs, widow, for example, is not to do anything until there is a project. permanent secular decline.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights the Walton family as the only ones who've held Walmart from 1970 till today, even after Sam Walton was gone.
claims.quote: So if I look at the Walton family, they are the only ones who've held Walmart from 1970 till today. They held it after Sam Walton was gone. They held it when there were no Walton's running the place.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the Google guys stepped aside but kept their stake, which is perfectly okay.
claims.quote: If we look at the Google guys, you know, they stepped aside. But they kept their stake. Perfectly okay.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Berkshire made a $2 billion investment in mid-American energy, which is today approaching $100 billion, and their railroad investment is huge.
claims.quote: And the way I look at it with Berkshire is they made a $2 billion investment in mid-American energy, which is today approaching $100 billion. It's a 50-bagger. Their railroad investment is huge.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Berkshire is sitting on $130, $140 billion and there's $30 billion a year coming in.
claims.quote: And they're sitting on, you know, $130, $140 billion. And there's $30 billion a year coming in.

claims.claim: The speaker discusses investing in Turkey, noting the ratio of GDP to market cap and the high inflation that was going to persist.
claims.quote: But what caught my eye in Turkey in 2018 was their ratio of GDP to market cap. GDP to market cap is not a, you know, you know, it's not something you can always hang your hat on. But there is a correlation, you know, you know, basically, you know, basically a a certain amount of the country's wealth is in the publicly traded companies.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that in Turkey, the P.E. was 0.1, meaning the company is going to earn its entire market cap in one month.
claims.quote: He tells me, the Mornish, the P.E. is 0.1. Not a P.E. of one. A 0.1 means that the company is going to earn its entire market gap in one month.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that they invested in a warehouse company in Turkey where the liquidation value was like six or seven hundred million in the market cap.
claims.quote: We invested in a warehouse company. I still couldn't believe it, but liquidation value was like six or seven hundred million in the market cap was spending money.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that they have three investments in Turkey after probably having visited about 80 or 90 businesses there over the years.
claims.quote: And I had a lot of cover because my friend knew the families, knew where the skeletons were. I mean, And he really studied these businesses a lot. And so I had, like, a great unpaid analyst on the ground. We didn't do a whole lot. I mean, if I look today, I made so many trips to Turkey, we have three investments. That's it.

claims.claim: The speaker discusses that one of the investments in Turkey gets a tailwind from inflation because their revenues are in euros and all the costs are in Lira.
claims.quote: Like, one of them gets a tailwind from because their revenues are in euros and all the costs are in Lira. So they actually get tail-ins from inflation. And they were very strong businesses.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that they have a view that the currency would continue to devalue quite significantly and inflation would be high.
claims.quote: Well, we, we had a view that the currency would continue to devalue quite significantly. Inflation would be high. It wouldn't go down in any, you know, you know, finite period of time.
